officialDocument.publisher: Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education (Curriculum Development and Technical Services) / Zimbabwe School Examinations Council (ZIMSEC)

sourceNote: Topic headings (section 6.0 and the scope and sequence, 7.0) and the competency-matrix sub-topic headings with their numbering (8.1 to 8.21) are transcribed from the Ministry's Biology Syllabus Forms 3 - 4 (2015 - 2022); verify them against a clean copy of the official document. Learning-objective statements are our own paraphrase of the competency matrix; their codes add .n to the sub-topic code. Each topic node gathers its Form 3 and Form 4 sub-topics.
notes: Source status (checked 2026-10-07): the official syllabus document ('Zimbabwe Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Biology Syllabus Forms 3 - 4, 2015 - 2022', Curriculum Development and Technical Services) was read through a text rendering of the provincial copy at http://www.mopsemashwest.gov.zw/files/MTB%20Bio.pdf, whose https certificate has expired. The topic list, the competency-matrix sub-topic headings and numbers, the objectives and content of every sub-topic, and the assessment section were read several times with consistent results, but the text rendering of tables can drop words, so absence of an item is less certain than its presence. Verify every heading and objective against a clean copy, and replace the officialDocument URL if a better official copy is found.
Subject code: not printed in the syllabus document; confirm the ZIMSEC code for this syllabus (code left null).

Version dates: assumed first examined in November 2018 (effectiveFrom 2018-01-01), in line with the Mathematics 2015-2022 file. Under the Heritage-Based Curriculum (2024-2030) new syllabi were issued; learners in Form 4 in 2025 were still examined on the 2015-2022 framework. Confirm which syllabus the November 2026 and later O-Level Biology examinations use, set effectiveTo, and create a new version file for the Heritage-Based Biology syllabus when it replaces this one.

Structure: topics are numbered 1 to 11 as in the topic list (6.0). The competency matrix numbers Form 3 sub-topics 8.1.x to 8.11.x and Form 4 sub-topics 8.12.x to 8.21.x; there is no Form 4 matrix for Cells and cellular activities. Topic 1 is listed as 'Branches of Biology' in 6.0 and as 'Safety, Careers and Branches in Biology' in the scope and sequence.
Gaps in the matrix numbering as read: there is no 8.2.2 and no 8.6.2. Digestion, teeth, absorption and assimilation appear under 8.6.1 Nutrition. Confirm.

Cellular transport: the rows of 8.3.1 Plant and animal cells and 8.3.2 Cell specialisation do not mention diffusion, osmosis or active transport. 'Diffusion and active uptake' appear in absorption (8.6.1), a diffusion gradient in transpiration (8.5.3) and 'diffusion and pressure filtration' in exchange between capillaries and tissue fluid (8.6.5); the word 'osmosis' was not found. So the diffusion and active transport concept is covered on 8.6.1, and the osmosis concept on 8.5.3, where it explains water uptake, turgor and wilting. Confirm, and move them if a clean copy places them elsewhere.

Not found in the copy read, so these concepts of the biology-o family are covered for Cambridge only: characteristics of living organisms, binomial naming and dichotomous keys, features of vertebrate and arthropod groups, magnification calculations, protein synthesis, sex linkage, adaptive features of hydrophytes and xerophytes (other than leaf adaptations that reduce transpiration) and methods of increasing food production. If the official document includes any of them, add the concept to the matching node.
Mitosis and meiosis are mentioned only in 8.6.7 Reproduction in humans (gamete formation and development of the zygote, details not required); the shared concept is covered there.
Terminology: ZIMSEC uses 'geotropism' where Cambridge uses 'gravitropism'.

Assessment (9.0) as read: continuous assessment 40% (practical tests, theory tests and end-of-term examinations in Forms 3 and 4) and a summative examination 60% of three papers. The stated paper weightings (30%, 40%, 30%) are recorded in assessmentOverview but not in the components because they refer to the summative examination; continuous assessment learning activities were later discontinued under the Heritage-Based Curriculum (replaced by school-based projects), so confirm the current scheme. Calculator rules are not stated.

Named examples in the matrix (as read): crop pests and diseases (tissue-eating and sap-sucking pests, bacterial wilt, rust; control with reference to maize, cotton and tobacco), livestock diseases (anthrax, foot-and-mouth disease, liver fluke, redwater; dosing, vaccination, dipping, quarantine), sexually transmitted infections (gonorrhoea, syphilis, chancroid, genital warts, genital herpes, HIV and AIDS), medicinal drugs (penicillin, paracetamol, aspirin and the antimalarials chloroquine and paludrine) and misused drugs (alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, solvents). Content should use current, well-established facts (e.g. chloroquine is no longer a recommended malaria treatment in Zimbabwe because of resistance) and be checked by a specialist teacher.
overview: ZIMSEC O-Level Biology is a two-year course for Forms 3 and 4. It develops knowledge, understanding and practical skills in biochemistry, cell biology, plant and animal (including human) structure and physiology, microbiology and biotechnology, genetics, biodiversity, ecology, and health and disease, using local organisms, crops, livestock and health issues so that learners can apply biology to their own lives, to further study and careers, and to Zimbabwe's sustainable development.
assessmentOverview: In the 2015 syllabus document the final assessment combines continuous assessment (40%: practical tests, theory tests and end-of-term examinations during Forms 3 and 4) with a summative ZIMSEC examination (60%) of three papers: Paper 1 (1 hour; 40 compulsory multiple-choice items; 40 marks; 30% of the examination), Paper 2 (2 hours; 100 marks; Section A: six compulsory structured questions of 10 marks each; Section B: four questions chosen from six, 10 marks each; 40%) and Paper 3 (a practical examination of 1 hour 30 minutes with two compulsory questions; 40 marks; 30%). Papers 1 and 2 assess knowledge and comprehension (60%) and handling information and solving problems (40%); Paper 3 assesses experimental skills. Continuous assessment learning activities were later replaced by school-based projects under the Heritage-Based Curriculum: confirm the current scheme with ZIMSEC.

components.name: Paper 2: Theory
components.description: Section A: six compulsory structured questions (60 marks). Section B: four questions chosen from six (40 marks).

topics.name: Safety, careers and branches in biology
topics.description: Listed as 'Branches of Biology' in the syllabus topic list (6.0).

objectives.text: Identify the causes of laboratory accidents (fire, fumes, acids and alkalis, microorganisms, misuse of apparatus, electricity) and apply safety rules, fire drills, emergency procedures and first aid.
Identify the branches of biology, such as cytology, anatomy, physiology, ecology, genetics, biotechnology, microbiology, zoology and botany, and what each studies.
Describe careers that use biology, such as medicine, research, ecology and conservation, and dietetics.
Identify and interpret hazard symbols and safety labels on containers of chemicals.

Describe the composition of water and relate its properties (solvent, transparency, high specific heat capacity) to its roles in organisms, such as in photosynthesis, temperature regulation and as a habitat.

children.name: Carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids

objectives.text: State the elements in carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids and the smaller units they are built from (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol, nucleotides).
Carry out the iodine, Benedict's, biuret and emulsion tests to identify starch, reducing sugars, proteins and lipids.
Classify carbohydrates as monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides and describe the uses of glucose, sucrose, starch, glycogen and cellulose in organisms.
Describe the functions of proteins in organisms, such as enzymes, structural proteins, transport and immunity.
Describe the functions of lipids, such as energy storage, cell membranes and insulation.
Describe the roles of DNA and RNA in inheritance and protein synthesis.

topics.name: Cells and cellular activities
topics.description: Form 3 only (there is no Form 4 matrix for this topic).

objectives.text: Describe the cell as the structural and functional unit of life, observe plant and animal cells with a microscope or bioviewer, and draw and label them.
Identify the nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, vacuole, cell wall, mitochondrion and chloroplast, state their functions and compare plant and animal cells.
Identify specialised cells (palisade cells, root hair cells, neurones, red and white blood cells, muscle cells, sperm and ova) and relate their structure to their functions.
Define enzymes as biological catalysts made of protein and investigate their properties, including specificity, using enzymes such as amylase and catalase.
Explain how enzymes work using the lock-and-key hypothesis.
Investigate and explain the effects of temperature and pH on enzyme activity.
Explain the use of enzymes in industry and the home, such as proteases and lipases in biological washing powders.
Define photosynthesis, state its word equation, investigate the conditions it needs (chlorophyll, light, carbon dioxide) and explain its importance in ecosystems.
Investigate how light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature affect the rate of photosynthesis, as limiting factors.
Relate the structure of the leaf to photosynthesis, and investigate gaseous exchange in plants and the distribution of stomata.
Describe the roles of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in plant growth and the signs of their deficiency.
Define biomass and productivity and explain how light, mineral salts, temperature, water, pests and diseases affect plant productivity.

Identify tissue-eating and sap-sucking pests and plant diseases (such as bacterial wilt and rust), explain how they reduce yields, and describe the advantages and disadvantages of management, cultural, chemical and biological control, with reference to crops such as maize, cotton and tobacco.

children.name: Transport
children.description: Form 3. Osmosis is also covered here: the syllabus does not name it, but it explains water uptake, turgor and wilting (see the syllabus notes).

objectives.text: Describe the external structure of a flowering plant, distinguish monocotyledons from dicotyledons, and compare the internal structure of roots and stems (epidermis, cortex, vascular tissue, pith).
State the functions of xylem (transport and support) and phloem (transport).

Define transpiration and describe its functions, investigate the factors that affect its rate (surface area, distribution of stomata, temperature, wind, humidity, light intensity), and describe leaf adaptations that reduce water loss and the significance of wilting.
Define translocation and describe the effects of ring-barking.
Describe natural methods (rhizomes, tubers, suckers, runners, bulbs) and artificial methods (cuttings, grafting) of asexual reproduction in plants and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.

Describe the structure of insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers, pollination, the advantages and disadvantages of self- and cross-pollination, and fertilisation after growth of the pollen tube.
Describe the formation of seeds and fruits, the methods and importance of seed dispersal, and the structure of monocotyledonous (maize) and dicotyledonous (bean) seeds.
Investigate the conditions needed for germination (water, oxygen, a suitable temperature) and describe the roles of enzymes in germination.
Define and illustrate phototropism and geotropism as responses of plants to light and gravity.
Define plant hormones and describe the uses of auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins and ethylene in controlling growth and development, including commercial applications.

children.name: Nutrition
children.description: Form 3. Includes digestion, teeth, absorption and assimilation (no separate 8.6.2 heading was found).

objectives.text: Describe a balanced diet, the sources and functions of nutrients, and how nutrient requirements vary with age, sex and activity.
Describe malnutrition, including deficiency diseases and the effects of too much fat and carbohydrate.

Identify the regions of the alimentary canal and the associated organs, state their functions and describe ingestion, mechanical digestion, peristalsis, chemical digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion.
Describe the actions of amylase, protease and lipase and the roles of hydrochloric acid, rennin and bile.
Describe how the small intestine is adapted for absorption, absorption by diffusion and active uptake, the role of the hepatic portal vein and the roles of the large intestine.
Define assimilation and outline the roles of the liver in metabolism, such as regulating glucose and amino acids, breaking down alcohol and toxins, and storing glycogen, fat and vitamins A and D.
Describe the types, functions and structure of teeth, the causes of tooth decay and how teeth are cared for.
State the functions of the parts of the respiratory system and describe the mechanism of breathing in and out.
Describe the structure of the alveoli and the factors that make gaseous exchange efficient.
State the differences between inhaled and exhaled air and explain the effects of physical activity on breathing and pulse rate.
Describe the short-term and long-term effects of smoking on the respiratory system, such as damage to cilia, extra mucus, bronchitis, emphysema and lung cancer.
Define aerobic respiration, state its word equation, describe ATP as the energy currency and list the uses of energy in the body.
Define anaerobic respiration, state its word equations in plants or yeast and in animals, and describe lactic acid production, fatigue and oxygen debt in muscles during exercise.
Describe the parts of the circulatory system, the structure and working of the heart (cardiac cycle, valves), and compare the pulmonary and systemic circulations.
Relate the structure of arteries, veins and capillaries to their functions and describe the exchange of materials between capillaries and tissue fluid by diffusion and pressure filtration.
State the functions of red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets and plasma.
Identify the causes of high blood pressure and the risk factors for coronary heart disease.
Explain how the body defends itself against infection (skin, tears, blood clotting, white blood cells engulfing pathogens and making antibodies).

Describe natural and artificial active immunity (infection, vaccination) and natural and artificial passive immunity (antibodies from the mother, antiserum injections), and discuss the importance of immunisation.
Analyse the effects of HIV on the body's immune system.
Describe the structure and functions of the male and female reproductive systems, the formation of gametes (details of meiosis not required) and compare sperm and ova.
Outline the phases of the menstrual cycle, including ovulation and the roles of oestrogen and progesterone.

Describe the pathway of sperm, fertilisation, development of the zygote and implantation, the roles and limitations of the placenta, the functions of amniotic fluid, and the dangers of drugs, smoking and alcohol in pregnancy.
Explain the causes of infertility and describe methods of contraception.
Identify the causes, signs and symptoms of sexually transmitted infections (gonorrhoea, syphilis, chancroid, genital warts, genital herpes, HIV and AIDS) and discuss how STIs and HIV are controlled.
Describe food conversion efficiency as the relationship between the food an animal eats and its gain in mass.

Identify animal pests and diseases (such as anthrax, foot-and-mouth disease, liver fluke and redwater) and their causes, explain how they reduce productivity, and outline their prevention and control by dosing, vaccination, dipping and quarantine.

Define homeostasis, identify the parts of the skin and relate them to temperature regulation (temperature receptors, sweating, shivering, vasodilation, vasoconstriction), including the role of the brain (hypothalamus) and negative feedback.
Define excretion and state the substances excreted by the kidneys, lungs and skin.
Describe the structure and functions of the urinary system and the kidney (cortex, medulla, pelvis; urine formation, osmoregulation, pH regulation), and explain how a dialysis machine works.
Describe the structure of sensory, relay and motor neurones and a simple spinal reflex arc.
State the functions of the main regions of the brain (cerebrum, cerebellum, pituitary gland, hypothalamus, medulla oblongata).
Describe the structure of the eye and the functions of its parts, explain how images are focused on the retina, and describe short sight and long sight and how they are corrected.
Describe the structure of the ear and the functions of its parts in hearing and balance.
Define a hormone and explain the effects of adrenaline in 'fright, fight or flight' situations.
Describe the roles of insulin and glucagon in regulating blood glucose, the signs and symptoms of diabetes mellitus and how it is managed.
State the functions of the skeleton and identify the bones of the mammalian forelimb (scapula, humerus, radius, ulna) and hindlimb (pelvic girdle, femur, tibia, fibula).
Classify joints (hinge, ball-and-socket) by the movement they allow and explain how antagonistic flexor and extensor muscles move a hinge joint.

children.name: Characteristics, types and economic importance of microorganisms

objectives.text: Identify the main characteristics of viruses, bacteria and fungi.

Describe the economic importance of microorganisms, such as decomposition and bioremediation, yeast in bread and alcohol production, bacteria in making yoghurt, cheese and insulin, and fungi in making penicillin.
Define recombinant DNA, outline the production of insulin by genetically modified bacteria, and discuss the benefits and hazards of the technology.
Describe chromosomes as made of DNA carrying genes, and use the terms allele, dominant, recessive, genotype, phenotype, homozygous and heterozygous.
Use genetic diagrams and Punnett squares to predict the F1 and F2 results and ratios of monohybrid crosses with complete dominance.
Explain codominance and the inheritance of the ABO blood groups, and the determination of sex by X and Y chromosomes.
Describe gene mutations (such as sickle-cell anaemia and albinism) and chromosome mutations (such as Down syndrome), and factors that increase the rate of mutation, such as radiation and carcinogens.

Identify variable characteristics of plants and animals (such as leaf size, pod size, height, coat colour, mass, tongue rolling and sex), and record and graph their distributions to distinguish continuous from discontinuous variation.
Define evolution and explain natural selection in terms of variation, competition, survival of the better adapted and reproduction.
Describe how and why artificial selection is used to improve crops and livestock, for example for productivity, quality and resistance to drought and disease.

children.name: Biodiversity
children.description: Form 3. Classification of organisms (the scope and sequence calls this sub-topic 'Classification').

objectives.text: Classify organisms into the five kingdoms (Prokaryotae, Protoctista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia) using their characteristic features.
Describe threats to biodiversity: deforestation, invasive species, habitat destruction, climate change and pollution.
Describe conservation measures, such as afforestation, the use of alternative sources of energy and the protection of endangered species.
Define an ecosystem and list its physical and biological components.
Describe the role of soil in ecosystems, its biological components (litter, earthworms, nematodes, termites, fungi, bacteria, humus) and their functions.
Compare clay, loam and sandy soils by experiment (particle size, aeration, water-holding capacity, drainage, leaching, pH).
Construct and interpret food chains and food webs using trophic levels (producers, consumers, decomposers).
Explain how energy is lost along food chains (respiration, heat) and interpret pyramids of numbers, biomass and energy.
Describe the carbon and nitrogen cycles.
Compare species diversity in natural and artificial ecosystems and discuss the problems of low diversity, such as loss of soil fertility and pest outbreaks.

Describe the advantages of ground cover (keeping topsoil, retaining water, reducing evaporation), identify harmful agricultural, mining, industrial and social activities and suggest corrective measures.

Explain carrying capacity and the limiting factors that set it (water, food, oxygen, space, shelter), and describe the effects of exceeding it, such as degradation, overgrazing, disease and pollution.

Define health as physical, mental, emotional and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease, and discuss personal, domestic and community hygiene, including waste disposal, clean drinking water, sanitation and health facilities.

Define disease, state its causes (infection, genetic defects, chemicals, radiation, malnutrition, degeneration) and classify diseases as infectious or non-infectious (deficiency diseases, genetic diseases, cancer).
Describe the causes, transmission, symptoms, prevention and control of cholera, malaria, tuberculosis, typhoid and bilharzia.
Define a drug and describe the medical uses of drugs such as antibiotics, analgesics and antimalarials.
Describe the physical, mental and social effects of misusing drugs such as alcohol, tobacco, cannabis and solvents.

topics.name: Experimental skills
topics.description: Not one of the eleven syllabus topics: groups the practical and experimental skills that the syllabus objectives require and that Paper 3 (practical examination) and the practical tests of continuous assessment assess. Practical-skills content is tagged here.

objectives.text: Handle apparatus, specimens and chemicals safely and accurately, and follow instructions.
Plan and carry out investigations, controlling variables and using control experiments.
Make and record observations and measurements, draw biological specimens, present results in tables and graphs, interpret them and evaluate procedures.
